name: Amharic
family: Afro-Asiatic, Semitic, South Semitic (Ethiosemitic), South Ethiopic
variety: Standard Amharic of Addis Ababa, as described by Hayward & Hayward (1992) from a speaker from Gondar
sources: Hayward, Katrina & Hayward, Richard J. (1992). Amharic. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 22: 48-52. Reprinted in the Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, Cambridge University Press, 1999.
Leslau, Wolf (1995). Reference Grammar of Amharic. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz.
Hudson, Grover (1997). Amharic and Argobba. In Robert Hetzron (ed.), The Semitic Languages. London: Routledge.
Demolin, Didier (2004). Acoustic and aerodynamic characteristics of ejectives in Amharic. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 115: 2610 (abstract).
Seid, Hussien, Rajendran, S. & Yegnanarayana, B. (2009). Acoustic characteristics of ejectives in Amharic. Proceedings of Interspeech 2009, Brighton.
Alemayehu Haile (1987). Lexical stress in Amharic. Journal of Ethiopian Studies 20.
contrasts: three-way laryngeal contrast in stops and affricates: voiceless (moderately aspirated), voiced, ejective
consonant gemination, lexical and grammatical (alə 'he said' against allə 'there is'), not shown in the script
labialised against plain consonants, mainly before /a/
two central vowels /ɨ/ and /ə/ against five peripheral vowels
/p pʼ pʷʼ/ occur in loanwords only; /ʔ/ is marginal
allophony: /p t tʃ k kʷ/ are moderately aspirated
voiced obstruents are devoiced before pause and before a voiceless obstruent: /lɨbs/ is [lɨps]
/b/ is an approximant [β] medially between sonorants
/sʼ/ is most commonly an affricate [tsʼ] and tends to merge with /tʼ/, most of all word-initially
ejective stops have a louder burst than the pulmonic stops; the ejective fricative has shorter noise followed by a glottal lag of about 30 ms (Demolin 2004)
single /r/ is a tap, geminate /rr/ a trill
consonants are strongly palatalised before /i/ and above all before /e/: /ɡize/ is [ɡʲizʲe]
/h/ is voiced between vowels and may be heard only as breathy voice on the vowels; after /ɨ/ or /i/ it is a palatal fricative [ç]
after palato-alveolar and palatal consonants /ɨ/ and /ə/ are fronted towards [i] and [e]; after labialised consonants and /w/ they are retracted and rounded towards [u] and [o]
consonants before rounded vowels have anticipatory lip rounding
the diphthongs are sequences of /a/ or /ə/ with /j/ or /w/

a prothetic [ɨ] precedes word-initial /r/; an epenthetic [ɨ] may be inserted between a word-final consonant and a following word-initial consonant; [ɨ] may be devoiced and barely audible between voiceless consonants
consonants may be lengthened after a nasal
phonotactics: /ɨ/ is largely epenthetic: it breaks up sequences of three consonants and final clusters that are not allowed
final clusters of two consonants are allowed (/lɨbs/, /wɨdd/)
all consonants except /p pʷʼ tʷʼ h hʷ/ may be geminate; single and geminate /ɲ/ do not contrast
in non-final closed syllables and in final syllables closed by two consonants only the central vowels occur, not the peripheral /i e u o/

stress.rule: Stress is weak and its position variable (Hayward & Hayward 1992); prominence tends to fall on a heavy syllable (closed, or before a geminate) and otherwise early in the word, and its relation to gemination and intonation is not settled.
stress.cues: slight; small rises of pitch and intensity. Gemination and syllable weight are more audible than stress.

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none caused by stress; the central vowels /ɨ ə/ are short and /ɨ/ may be devoiced or dropped between voiceless consonants
rhythm.notes: The class is an impressionistic label based on the weak stress; no rhythm-metric study is cited. Geminate consonants must be kept long.

length.notes: Geminates contrast with single consonants in all positions except word-initially. The peripheral vowels /i e a o u/ are longer than the central /ɨ ə/ and can be prolonged in open syllables (Hayward & Hayward 1992). No duration ratio is given here.

intonation.declarative: gradual declination with a fall at the end; the verb is final and carries the last prominence
intonation.yes_no_question: rise on the last syllable, or a question particle such as wəj at the end of the sentence
intonation.wh_question: prominence on the question word, which stands before the verb; falling end
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of non-final clauses
intonation.notes: Amharic intonation is little studied; Hayward & Hayward (1992) say that stress and intonation need further investigation. These settings are provisional.

phonation: ejective stops, affricates and fricative (glottalic egressive airstream)
breathy voice as the realisation of /h/ between vowels

problems: Gemination is not written in the Ethiopic script and is never produced: አለ is [ʔalə] for both /alə/ 'he said' and /allə/ 'there is', አማርኛ has a single [ɲ].

Every sixth-order letter inside a word is given the vowel ɨ; only a word-final one after a vowel is left bare. ትምህርት gives [tɨmɨhɨrɨt] for [tɨmhɨrt], ይሰብራል gives [jɨsəβɨral] for [jɨsəbral], ቋንቋ gives [kʼʷanɨkʼʷa] for [kʼʷankʼʷa].
ጸ and ፀ are the plain affricate [ts], not the ejective /sʼ/ [tsʼ].
Only k` uses an ejective recording (ustop/k_ejc). p`, t` and tS` use unaspirated plosive samples after a pause, although p_ejc, t_ejc and c_ejc samples exist in phsource/ustop.
Stress is fixed on the first syllable, with the French stress lengths; the literature describes weak, variable stress.
Labialised consonants are consonant plus w sequences.
The IPA names of the ejectives are written with a grave accent (t`) instead of ʼ.
No devoicing of voiced obstruents before pause, no palatalisation before /e/.
good: seven vowels, with ɨ and ə
b is lenited to [β] between vowels
word-final h becomes a fricative, [ç] after i
ejectives are separate phonemes from the plain stops
ɲ, ʒ and the labialised velars are covered by the rules

notes: The two gaps that change words are the missing gemination and the over-inserted ɨ; both need a lexicon or morphological rules because the script does not mark them.
